lessons.title: Threads, lifecycle and the Java Memory Model
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Distinguish concurrent work from parallel execution and reason about shared memory.

A platform thread is backed by an operating-system thread. Calling `start()` schedules a new thread; directly calling `run()` is an ordinary method call. Thread states include NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED. RUNNABLE does not prove that a thread is currently on a CPU.

Three separate questions matter: **atomicity** (can an operation be interleaved?), **visibility** (when can another thread observe a write?), and **ordering** (which observations are guaranteed?). `count++` is a read-modify-write operation, so it needs coordination when shared.

A volatile write happens-before a subsequent read of that field. This is useful for a stop flag, but does not make an increment atomic. Releasing and acquiring the same monitor establishes visibility; thread start and successful join also provide ordering guarantees. Prefer immutable data and confinement when sharing is unnecessary.

## Practice
Write two workers that increment a shared counter 10,000 times each. Compare an unsafe integer, an AtomicInteger, and a synchronized counter. Join both workers before reading the result.

## Expected result and self-review
The coordinated versions must produce 20,000. The unsafe version might produce 20,000 too; one successful run does not prove safety. Explain why sleeping does not establish a happens-before relationship and why volatile alone does not fix the increment.

## References
- [Concurrency API and memory consistency](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html)

lessons.title: Executors, futures, cancellation and overload
Locks, conditions and deadlock prevention
Atomics, concurrent collections and coordination
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Match the coordination tool to the invariant you need.

AtomicInteger supports atomic single-value updates. Compare-and-set retries are appropriate for short side-effect-free update logic; retrying an external payment would not be safe. LongAdder is useful for contended statistics, but its sum is not an atomic snapshot suitable for enforcing a balance limit.

ConcurrentHashMap makes individual supported operations thread-safe. Use putIfAbsent or compute for a per-key transition rather than a separate containsKey and put. A cross-key invariant still needs broader coordination. Keep compute functions short and avoid external side effects.

A bounded BlockingQueue connects producers and consumers and can apply backpressure. A Semaphore limits simultaneous access to a scarce resource. CountDownLatch is a one-shot gate; CyclicBarrier supports repeated rendezvous. Phaser supports changing participation. Pick these based on lifecycle rather than familiarity.

## Practice
Implement a bounded job queue with two producers and three consumers. Define an explicit termination protocol, propagate worker failures, and ensure shutdown cannot leave a producer blocked forever. Separately implement per-book reservation using an atomic map operation.

## Self-review
Verify no lost or duplicated job IDs, correct empty-queue behavior, and bounded queue size under a slow consumer. Explain why a concurrent collection cannot automatically make a whole business transaction atomic.

## References
- [Concurrency utilities](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html)

lessons.title: Java 21 virtual threads and resource limits
CompletableFuture and structured concurrency boundaries
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Compose asynchronous results and distinguish stable Java 21 APIs from previews.

CompletableFuture can transform a result with thenApply, flatten dependent asynchronous work with thenCompose, and combine independent results with thenCombine. Non-async continuations can run in the completing thread. Async methods without an explicit executor generally use the common ForkJoinPool; do not casually put blocking service calls there.

Define failure propagation with exceptionally, handle, or whenComplete according to whether the stage recovers, transforms, or observes an outcome. A fallback must not silently turn an authentication failure into successful access. A CompletableFuture timeout does not guarantee cancellation of its underlying operation.

Structured concurrency groups child tasks within a parent lifetime and makes failure and cancellation policy explicit. **StructuredTaskScope and scoped values are preview APIs in Java 21.** Their API shape changes across releases. Study the lifecycle concepts first; ordinary examples in this pack do not require preview flags.

## Practice
Combine an account lookup and a notification-preferences lookup using explicit executors. Give each dependency an operation-level timeout. Define whether a preferences failure may use a default and whether an account failure fails the whole request.

## Self-review
Test success, partial failure, timeout, and interruption. Document where each stage executes and whether underlying work stops when the caller stops waiting. Explain what problem structured child-task lifetimes solve that simply collecting Futures does not.

## References
- [CompletableFuture and execution policies](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html)
- [Java 21 virtual-thread guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/core/virtual-threads.html)

lessons.title: JVM deep dive: class loading, memory and JIT
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Trace a program through loading and execution, then connect memory areas to failure symptoms.

Compilation produces class files. The JVM loads classes, verifies bytecode, links symbolic references, and initializes classes before applicable uses. Parent delegation is a common class-loader model, not a rule that every custom loader must follow. Class identity includes its defining loader, which matters for plugin isolation and apparent duplicate types.

Each platform thread has call frames holding local variables and operand stacks. Objects are managed on the heap; HotSpot stores class metadata in native metaspace and compiled machine code in a code cache. Virtual-thread stacks have a different implementation and can reside in heap stack chunks: avoid assuming one dedicated native stack per virtual thread.

HotSpot combines interpretation and just-in-time compilation. Profiling guides inlining and optimization; assumptions can later be invalidated and code deoptimized. Escape analysis may eliminate allocations, so an object in source does not guarantee a corresponding heap allocation in optimized execution.

## Diagnostic lab
Use a disposable application with a retained collection, a deep recursive call, and repeated hot-method calls as separate scenarios. Inspect bytecode with `javap -c ClassName`. Before inspecting a running process, list it with `jcmd -l`, then replace PID below with its actual number:

```text
jcmd PID VM.flags
jcmd PID GC.heap_info
jcmd PID Compiler.codecache
jcmd PID VM.classloader_stats
```

## Self-review
Distinguish stack overflow, heap exhaustion, metaspace growth, and native-memory exhaustion. Explain why process memory exceeds the Java heap and why warm-up affects timing. Record observations rather than assuming exact object sizes or one heap layout for every collector.

## References
- [Java 21 VM guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/vm/index.html)
- [jcmd diagnostic commands](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/jcmd.html)

lessons.title: GC deep dive: reachability, G1 and ZGC
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Explain reclamation and choose a collector using workload objectives.

GC starts from roots such as live thread references and traces reachable objects. An object that is no longer useful to the business can still be reachable through a cache or listener. GC does not fix that retention bug. Resource cleanup for files and connections belongs in deterministic lifecycle management, not a promise about when collection happens.

Collectors use combinations of marking, copying, compaction, and concurrent work. Stop-the-world phases pause application execution; concurrent phases also consume CPU. Generational strategies exploit different object lifetimes, but layouts differ: do not describe every collector as Eden, survivor, and old spaces.

G1 uses regions and aims to balance throughput and pause goals. Evacuation moves live objects; allocation pressure, large objects, and retained live data affect behavior. A pause target is a goal, not a guaranteed latency bound.

ZGC targets short pauses with concurrent work. In **Java 21**, generational ZGC is selected with `-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational`; do not assume those exact flags are appropriate for every later release. Serial and Parallel collectors can suit other footprint and throughput objectives.

## Practice
Choose a latency objective and throughput target. Replay the same bounded workload with the default collector, then one alternative available in your JDK. Hold heap and CPU budgets constant and report allocation rate, pause distribution, throughput, and live-set behavior after collection.

## Self-review
Explain why lower GC pauses do not necessarily mean lower request latency. Distinguish allocation churn from a rising retained live set. Report trade-offs and repeat measurements; avoid choosing a collector from one average.

## References
- [GC tuning guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/gctuning/index.html)
- [Collector selection](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/gctuning/available-collectors.html)

lessons.title: Performance lab: JFR, GC logs and memory budgets
lessons.content:
**Baseline:** Java 21, no preview features unless explicitly stated. **Prerequisites:** Java basics, collections, exceptions, and basic OOP.

## What you will learn
Investigate a symptom with evidence before changing runtime flags.

Start with an explicit symptom: high tail latency, low throughput, CPU saturation, growing resident memory, or blocked work. Record JDK build, collector, heap limits, container CPU/memory limits, input, concurrency, and warm-up. Compare equal workloads and separate server processing time from queueing and client latency.

For a local Java 21 application, enable bounded GC logging at startup:

```text
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=10M -jar app.jar
```

Inspect the actual process and start a short recording:

```text
jcmd -l
jcmd PID JFR.start name=baseline settings=profile duration=30s filename=baseline.jfr
jcmd PID Thread.print -l
```

Replace PID with the local process number. Use JDK Mission Control to correlate allocation, hot methods, blocking, and GC events. Diagnostics have overhead; assess commands on a test environment first. Thread.print helps inspect platform-thread locks; use virtual-thread-aware dumps such as `Thread.dump_to_file` when investigating virtual threads.

A container budget includes heap, metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers, GC structures, and other native memory. An explicit -Xmx fixes the heap cap; MaxRAMPercentage supplies an ergonomic percentage when an explicit maximum is absent. Do not add both expecting their limits to combine. Leave measured non-heap headroom.

## Practice and self-review
Compare a bounded cache and an intentionally retaining cache under the same load. Record the retained heap trend, request p95/p99, and process memory. Change one factor at a time and keep a results table. Use JMH for focused microbenchmarks; a stopwatch loop is vulnerable to warm-up, dead-code elimination, and allocation optimization.

## References
- [jcmd and recording options](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/jcmd.html)
- [GC tuning](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/gctuning/index.html)
- [JMH project](https://openjdk.org/projects/code-tools/jmh/)
